intro.title: The thinking behind the work.
intro.description: These stories follow the decisions behind the work: what I took ownership of, who I worked with, and what changed. Some led to a product. Others changed how the team could work.
intro.closing: There is always a better way, together we will find it.

studies.title: One platform. Five properties.
studies.summary: I owned the roadmap for a shared commerce platform. Launching a branded property went from six weeks to two.
studies.scope: Platform roadmap, brand experience, and the commerce funnel
studies.collaboration: A part-time engineer and I built and maintained the core framework. Other designers launched the properties; internal engineering supplied the microservices and APIs.
studies.source: docs/case-studies-sanitized.md: One Platform, Five Properties; docs/copy-register.md: Section A, DentalPlans; B79

proof.label: of company revenue growth in one measured year

atAGlance: Each new storefront would inherit the first site’s manual work.
I phased a shared platform around the capabilities later properties could reuse.
A branded property went from six weeks to launch to two. Five properties used the platform.

sections.label: The first site
sections.title: The first site sold. Its manual work would multiply.
paragraphs: The first storefront had sale pricing and strikethrough values typed in by hand, product by product, every time a promotion changed.

It answered the question it was built for: would customers buy through a focused brand experience? They did. Leadership wanted more properties, and copying the site would carry those updates into every new one.

sections.label: The roadmap
sections.title: I brought a roadmap for the work we could stop doing.
paragraphs: I argued for a platform and phased the work. Each release replaced a manual task with something the next property could reuse.

Brand settings moved into the content management layer. Shared product and provider data meant engineering could add information once and every property could use it. Scheduled promotions replaced hand-edited offers.

I owned the roadmap, experience, and front-end work for the core framework. A part-time engineer and I built and maintained it. Other designers launched the branded properties. The internal engineering team built the microservices and APIs we connected to.
sections.decision: Build the shared capability before repeating the task on another property.

sections.label: The platform
sections.title: Each brand kept its identity.
paragraphs: Theme tokens separated brand choices from the application. A property could change its visual identity without becoming another copy of the code to maintain.

Source attribution connected acquisition to the storefront. Promotion, copy, and messaging changed with the visitor’s source, down to individual affiliate identifiers. The page said what the ad promised.
Deployment could target one property or all of them. The same framework covered marketing pages through cart and checkout.
points: Brand identity as configuration
Shared product and provider data
Scheduled offers across the commerce flow
Deployment for one property or all of them

sections.label: What changed
sections.title: The next launch had a starting point.
paragraphs: Launching a fully branded property fell from six weeks to two. Five properties ran on the platform.

In one measured year, finance credited the properties with 47% of company revenue growth, 27% of total lead capture, and 20% of overall revenue. The growth figure is a share of the company’s revenue-growth increment in that year.
The company owned the custom platform. Its designers could spend more time on the parts that made each brand distinct, while the framework handled work the properties had in common.
sections.takeaway: You create velocity by making the work smaller.

studies.title: Building an experience design practice
studies.summary: I built a design practice alongside a product integration, leaving research, systems, and measurement the team could use again.
studies.scope: Design foundations, research, measurement, and executive facilitation
studies.collaboration: Work across product, engineering, marketing, and leadership.
studies.source: docs/case-studies-sanitized.md: Building the Function That Was Not There; Making UX Visible in the Numbers; Four Executives, Four Different Customer Journeys; docs/copy-register.md: B37
atAGlance: The integration started before the design practice existed.
I built reusable foundations inside the delivery work.
The team gained documented tokens, a research format, an experience scorecard, and workshop materials.

sections.label: The starting point
sections.title: Delivery could not wait for the practice.
paragraphs: There was no existing design system, research practice, or experience-measurement framework. The function had to take shape while a product integration moved forward.
Spending all our attention on the immediate screens would leave the next project with the same missing foundations.

sections.label: Building alongside delivery
sections.title: Where work repeated, I left something the team could use.
paragraphs: I built the token foundation before the page count grew. Usability testing came with a report format for later studies. Executive workshops had a board system, moderator guide, and scenario matrix.

Measurement needed its own structure. I paired experience measures with business outcomes and drew on real user monitoring, moderated testing, and survey data. Each source answered a different question.
sections.decision: Treat the foundations as part of delivering the product.

sections.label: The working practice
sections.title: Give the next person a starting point.
paragraphs: The team had documented tokens, a research-report format, an experience scorecard, and materials for executive workshops.
The customer feedback program had a vendor recommendation and was ready for instrumentation.
points: Documented design decisions
Research the next study could build on
Experience measures tied to business questions
Workshop materials available after the meeting

sections.label: What remained
sections.title: The work outlived the first project.
paragraphs: Subsequent work could use the foundations already written down. The team did not have to begin with an empty research report or invent another workshop format.
The artifact was stability. Portfolio photography remains challenging.

studies.title: Four executives, four different customer journeys.
studies.summary: I designed and ran a working session that put the owners of the customer journey in the same room to examine its handoffs.
studies.scope: Customer scenarios, the end-to-end journey, and cross-functional handoffs
studies.collaboration: Executive participants across marketing, digital health, engineering, and commerce.
studies.source: docs/case-studies-sanitized.md: Four Executives, Four Different Customer Journeys
atAGlance: Each department held only part of the journey.
The working session followed concrete customer situations across departments.
The group documented the end-to-end journey and examined the gaps with their owners present.

sections.label: The handoffs
sections.title: Customers had declined to organize themselves into departments.
paragraphs: The integration crossed marketing, digital health, engineering, and commerce. Each leader held a different part of the journey. No shared view covered first awareness through subscription and refill.
Where those views stopped, the customer changed hands. That was where we needed the conversation.

sections.label: The preparation
sections.title: I designed the conversation before the session.
paragraphs: I built a board system for the integration and wrote a moderator guide. The session needed enough structure to work without depending on my improvisation.
A scenario matrix kept the group on concrete customer situations. We could follow a person through the experience and examine what happened at each handoff.
sections.decision: Put the owners of both sides of a handoff in the same conversation.

sections.label: In the room
sections.title: Follow the customer, then examine the gap.
paragraphs: I used the scenarios to walk the group through the journey. When a handoff failed, the people responsible for both sides were present to discuss it.
The moderator guide kept the discussion on the customer situation and the work between departments.
points: A board system for the integration
Concrete customer scenarios
Both sides of the handoff present

sections.label: The record
sections.title: A journey the group could return to.
paragraphs: The session produced a documented end-to-end journey and a record of the gaps discussed. The boards, guide, and scenario matrix remained available for later sessions.

studies.title: How customers look for products
studies.summary: I led customer research into navigation and used the findings to guide category structure and shop-by paths.
studies.scope: Navigation, category structure, and shop-by paths
studies.collaboration: Research findings prepared for the team making navigation and information-architecture decisions.
studies.source: docs/case-studies-sanitized.md: Navigation Decisions Were Being Made on Taste

proof.label: an entry point into the catalog

atAGlance: Navigation decisions depended on internal preference.
Moderated testing examined how people entered the catalog and used the menu.
The findings informed the redesign and left a repeatable research-report format.

sections.label: The question
sections.title: We knew the catalog. Our customers did not.
paragraphs: Category structure, mega menu choices, and shop-by paths were being debated internally. They had not been tested against people using the navigation.
Knowing where a product lives changes how easy it looks to find. We needed to see the experience without that advantage.

sections.label: The study
sections.title: Watch where people try to enter.
paragraphs: I led moderated usability research into the navigation and information architecture. The study examined entry paths and whether people could discover and use the mega menu.
sections.decision: Use observed behavior to guide the catalog’s entry points.

sections.label: The findings
sections.title: The customer’s need was a useful starting point.
paragraphs: Testing supported Shop by Condition as an entry point. It also exposed discoverability problems in the mega menu.
I brought those findings into the redesign and organized the report around the decisions the team needed to make.
points: Shop by Condition as an entry point
Menu-discovery problems documented
Findings attached to design decisions

sections.label: What changed
sections.title: Preference lost its monopoly.
paragraphs: The team had observed customer behavior to work from. It also had a research-report format for the next study.

studies.title: A shared foundation for a second brand
studies.shortTitle: A shared foundation for a second brand
studies.summary: I defined the brand rules and documented the shared design foundation before the page count grew.
studies.scope: Theme tokens, brand treatment, button variants, and component evaluation
studies.collaboration: A documented foundation for the next designer and the shared commerce build.
atAGlance: A second brand needed a home on a platform without a design system.
I defined theme tokens and the rules for using them before more pages were built.
The brand launched on shared infrastructure with a documented foundation for later design work.

sections.label: Before the pages
sections.title: Every page could become another place to fix the brand.
paragraphs: A second brand needed to live inside an existing commerce platform. There was no design system.
If each page carried its own styles, every brand adjustment would require another search through pages and files.

sections.label: The shared decisions
sections.title: Decide what the pages should inherit.
paragraphs: I defined color, typography, and spacing tokens, then layered the brand over that base. Button variants had documented accessibility constraints.
I evaluated a component foundation and recorded the recommendation and reasoning. The next designer needed more than a set of unexplained values.
sections.decision: Document the shared decisions before they spread across the interface.

sections.label: The foundation
sections.title: Give the brand a place to change.
paragraphs: The theme separated brand choices from the underlying platform. Tokens and button variants had a documented foundation that another designer could use.
Accessibility constraints were recorded with those decisions. They did not replace testing the finished experience.
points: Base tokens for shared choices
A brand theme over the base
Accessibility constraints with button variants
A component recommendation with its reasoning

sections.label: The handoff
sections.title: The next designer inherited the reasoning.
paragraphs: The brand launched on the shared infrastructure. Brand adjustments could happen at the token layer, and the next designer had the decisions and their reasoning documented.

studies.title: Four documents, one checkout, zero agreement.
studies.discipline: Experience strategy · AI-assisted analysis · Decision ownership
studies.summary: I resolved conflicting checkout requirements and recorded the decision engineering should build. AI compared the sources; I owned the call.
studies.scope: Checkout price presentation and requirements reconciliation
studies.collaboration: Engineering and product stakeholders working from conflicting written requirements.
studies.source: docs/case-studies-sanitized.md: Four Documents, One Checkout, Zero Agreement

proof.label: engineering built from the recorded decision

atAGlance: Written requirements disagreed on how to present the consult fee.
I compared the sources with AI, chose the experience, and recorded what the decision replaced.
Engineering built against the decision without another meeting cycle. Refund messaging remained an open dependency.

sections.label: The conflict
sections.title: Both versions were written down. Both looked current.
paragraphs: Requirements called for an itemized consult fee. The latest meeting directive and the design called for one combined price. Engineering could build either and point to a written source.
The disagreement would change what a customer saw beside the Buy button. It needed an owner and a decision.

sections.label: The decision
sections.title: Read the sources together, then make the call.
paragraphs: I used AI to compare the requirements, meeting transcripts, and ticket history. Reading the records together exposed the contradictions.
I chose a combined price, matching a checkout pattern already converting with customers. AI identified the contradictions; the experience decision was mine.
sections.decision: Use a combined price and identify the requirements it supersedes.

sections.label: The record
sections.title: Give engineering something it can build against.
paragraphs: I documented the combined-price direction and linked the superseded requirements to their sources. The record explained what changed and why.
Refund messaging remained a dependency. It needed to match the price model so the next part of the experience did not contradict the checkout.
points: Combined-price direction recorded
Superseded requirements linked to sources
Refund messaging left as an explicit dependency

sections.label: After the decision
sections.title: The record held the answer.
paragraphs: Engineering built against the recorded direction without another meeting cycle. Refund messaging remained open.
